linear-rotational-link-s2.title: String pulled off a spool
linear-rotational-link-s2.text: A string is wound on a spool of radius 0.025 m that turns on a fixed axle. A student pulls the string so it comes off the spool without slipping. A rotation sensor records the angle the spool has turned, starting from rest.

items.q: What is the speed of the valve while the wheel turns at 12 rad/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides ω by r. Speed is v = rω: multiply.
Value: that uses the reflector’s distance, 0.20 m. The valve is 0.33 m from the axle.

why.correct: v = rω = (0.33 m)(12 rad/s) = 3.96 m/s, about 4.0 m/s. The radian drops out of the unit.

items.q: Compared with the valve, the reflector has
options: the same angular velocity and a smaller speed
the same speed and a smaller angular velocity
a larger angular velocity and the same speed
the same angular velocity and the same speed

why.correct: The wheel is rigid, so both share ω = 12 rad/s. Speed is v = rω, so the reflector (0.20 m) moves at 2.4 m/s and the valve (0.33 m) at about 4.0 m/s.
options: Right: one ω for the whole wheel, and v = rω is smaller at smaller r.
Every point on the wheel shares ω; it is the speed that depends on r.
Points closer to the axle do not turn faster; ω is shared.
The reflector traces a smaller circle in the same time, so it moves more slowly.

items.q: While the wheel slows steadily to rest, what is the size of the valve’s tangential acceleration?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the centripetal acceleration rω² at 12 rad/s. The tangential acceleration is rα.
Value: that is the angular acceleration in rad/s². Multiply by r to get the tangential acceleration.

why.correct: α = Δω/Δt = 12 rad/s ÷ 6.0 s = 2.0 rad/s² in size, so a_T = rα = (0.33 m)(2.0 rad/s²) = 0.66 m/s².

items.q: How far does the valve travel along its circle while the wheel slows from 12 rad/s to rest?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses 12 rad/s for the whole 6.0 s. The wheel slows steadily, so its average ω is 6.0 rad/s.
Value: that is the angle turned, in radians. Multiply by r for the distance: s = rθ.

why.correct: With steady slowing, the average ω is (12 + 0)/2 = 6.0 rad/s, so Δθ = (6.0 rad/s)(6.0 s) = 36 rad and s = rθ = (0.33 m)(36 rad) = 11.9 m, about 12 m.

items.q: If the wheel turned at 24 rad/s instead of 12 rad/s, the valve’s speed would be
options: 2 times as large
4 times as large
the same
half as large

why.correct: v = rω with r fixed at 0.33 m, so v ∝ ω: doubling ω doubles v (to about 7.9 m/s).
options: Right: v = rω, so v is proportional to ω at fixed r.
v = rω has no square; doubling ω doubles v.
The valve stays at 0.33 m, so a larger ω means a larger speed.
A faster wheel moves the valve faster, not slower.

items.q: How much string has come off the spool after 4.0 s?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides the angle by r. The length is s = rθ.
Value: that treats the 32.0 rad as 32 revolutions. The sensor gives radians, so s = rθ directly.

why.correct: The string leaves the rim, so its length equals the distance along the rim: s = rθ = (0.025 m)(32.0 rad) = 0.80 m.

items.q: The data fit θ = (2.0 rad/s²)t². What is the string’s acceleration?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses 2.0 rad/s² as α. Compare with θ = ½αt²: ½α = 2.0 rad/s², so α = 4.0 rad/s².

why.correct: θ = ½αt² = (2.0 rad/s²)t² gives α = 4.0 rad/s². The string’s acceleration equals the rim’s tangential acceleration: a = rα = (0.025 m)(4.0 rad/s²) = 0.10 m/s².

items.q: Which graph of the string’s speed against time fits the data?
options: A straight line rising from the origin
A horizontal line above zero
A curve that gets steeper with time
A straight line falling to zero

why.correct: θ ∝ t² means constant α from rest, so ω = αt and the string’s speed v = rω = rαt: a straight line through the origin with slope rα.
options: Right: constant α gives constant a = rα, so v grows steadily from zero.
A flat speed graph means no acceleration, but the angle grows faster each second.
That would need a growing acceleration; here α is constant.
The spool starts from rest and speeds up.

items.q: The string comes off the spool without slipping. Which two quantities are equal?
options: The string’s speed and the speed of the spool’s rim
The string’s speed and the spool’s angular velocity
The string’s acceleration and the spool’s angular acceleration
The string’s length and the spool’s angle

why.correct: Where the string leaves the rim they move together, so the string’s speed equals the rim’s speed rω, its acceleration equals rα, and its length equals rθ.
options: Right: no slipping means the string and the rim move together where they touch.
These have different units (m/s and rad/s); they are linked by v = rω, not equal.
Different units again: a = rα links them.
The length pulled off is s = rθ, not θ itself.

items.q: The tip of a ceiling-fan blade is 0.60 m from the axis and moves at 9.0 m/s. What is the fan’s angular velocity?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies v by r. From v = rω, ω = v/r.

items.q: In s = rθ and v = rω, the angle and angular velocity have to be in radians because
options: the radian is defined so that distance along a circle equals rθ
degrees are not SI units of length
the equations are on the equations sheet in radians
radians make the numbers smaller

why.correct: θ in radians is (distance along the circle)/r, so s = rθ is just the definition rearranged. In degrees you would need an extra factor of π/180.
options: Right: a radian is the angle where the distance equals the radius.
Neither radians nor degrees are units of length; the reason is how the radian is defined.
The sheet uses radians because of the definition, not the reverse.
The size of the numbers has nothing to do with it.

items.q: A Ferris wheel of radius 15 m makes one revolution every 60 s. What is the speed of a rider?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides r by the period. In one period the rider covers the whole circumference, 2πr.
Value: that is the circumference, a distance. Divide by the 60 s period.

why.correct: ω = 2π rad / 60 s = 0.105 rad/s, so v = rω = (15 m)(0.105 rad/s) = 1.57 m/s, about 1.6 m/s.

items.q: A belt joins a small pulley (radius 0.10 m) to a large pulley (radius 0.30 m) without slipping. The small pulley turns at 30 rad/s. How fast does the large pulley turn?
options: 10 rad/s
90 rad/s
30 rad/s
3.3 rad/s

why.correct: The belt moves at one speed, which equals each rim’s speed: v = (0.10 m)(30 rad/s) = 3.0 m/s. The large pulley then turns at ω = v/r = 3.0/0.30 = 10 rad/s.
options: Right: the belt gives both rims the same speed, 3.0 m/s, so ω = 3.0/0.30.
This multiplies by the ratio of radii the wrong way; the larger pulley turns more slowly.
The pulleys are not one rigid body; the belt links their rim speeds, not their ω.
This divides by 9, as if speed scaled with r². Rim speed v = rω is linear in r.

items.q: A point on the rim of a grinding wheel of radius 0.40 m has a tangential acceleration of 2.0 m/s². What is the wheel’s angular acceleration?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies a_T by r. From a_T = rα, α = a_T/r.

items.q: A turntable spins at a constant angular velocity. A beetle walks slowly from the rim straight in to a point halfway to the center. Predict how each quantity for the beetle changes.

variables.name: Its angular velocity
variables.why: The beetle turns with the turntable, which keeps the same ω at every radius.

variables.name: Its speed around the circle
variables.why: v = rω, and r halves while ω stays the same, so the speed halves.

variables.name: Its centripetal acceleration
variables.why: a_c = v²/r = rω², so at the same ω it is proportional to r and halves.

why.correct: ω is shared by the whole turntable. Speed v = rω and centripetal acceleration rω² are both proportional to r, so both fall as the beetle moves inward.

items.q: A turntable speeds up with constant angular acceleration. A point at distance r from the axis has tangential acceleration a. A point at distance 3r has tangential acceleration
options: 3a
9a
a

why.correct: Every point shares α, and a_T = rα, so tripling r triples the tangential acceleration.
options: Right: a_T = rα with α shared, so a_T ∝ r.
a_T = rα has no square in r.
α is shared, but a_T also depends on r.
Points farther out speed up more, not less.
